blocks.text: A 34-year-old man and his 31-year-old wife have been trying to conceive for two years. His semen analysis shows a sperm concentration of 8 million/mL and total motility of 25%.

items.text: Explain the purpose of semen analysis.
Describe correct specimen collection.
Interpret the results.
Outline further investigations and management.

blocks.text: Alternative scenarios

items.text: A semen analysis showing azoospermia.
A patient with low semen volume.
A report showing reduced sperm motility.
A patient asking whether one abnormal result means permanent infertility.
A couple asking whether IVF or ICSI will be necessary.

blocks.text: Semen analysis is a laboratory examination of an ejaculate to assess its physical characteristics and sperm parameters.

items.text: Assess male reproductive function during infertility investigations.
Identify abnormalities in sperm concentration, number, motility and morphology.
Guide further male reproductive investigations.
Help determine appropriate treatment options.
Assess semen after selected procedures, such as vasectomy, according to the relevant protocol.

blocks.text: A semen analysis is not a complete fertility test. It does not directly measure every aspect of sperm function, fertilisation potential or the likelihood of natural conception.
This is a common counselling station. You should explain the procedure clearly and reassure the patient about privacy and confidentiality.

items.text: Follow the laboratory's instructions regarding abstinence, commonly 2–7 days before collection.
Wash hands and clean the genital area according to laboratory instructions.
Collect the sample by masturbation into a clean, laboratory-approved container.
Avoid ordinary lubricants and standard condoms unless the laboratory provides a validated sperm-safe collection method.
Collect the entire ejaculate. Report any spillage or loss of the initial fraction, which may contain a high proportion of sperm.
Label the specimen correctly and record the collection time and other details requested by the laboratory.
Deliver the sample within the laboratory's specified time, following its transport and temperature instructions. Many laboratories aim to assess it within about one hour.
Inform the laboratory of a recent febrile illness, incomplete collection or other relevant circumstances.

content_groups.group_title: What if the patient cannot produce a sample?

blocks.text: Explore the difficulty sensitively and discuss options with the laboratory or fertility specialist. Depending on the circumstances, an approved collection method, collection at the laboratory, or selected assisted collection techniques may be possible.
Do not recommend ordinary condoms or unvalidated lubricants because they may affect sperm motility.
Why is abstinence recommended before semen collection?

The abstinence interval standardises specimen collection and influences semen volume and sperm parameters. Excessively short or long intervals can affect results, so the laboratory's recommended interval should be followed consistently.
Semen analysis evaluates several parameters. Learn the following WHO 6th-edition lower fifth-percentile reference values.
WHO reference values — sixth edition, 2021
Semen volume
Lower reference limit
Sperm concentration
Lower reference limit
Total sperm number
Per ejaculate
Total motility
Lower reference limit
Progressive motility
Lower reference limit
Normal morphology
Lower reference limit
Sperm vitality
Lower reference limit for live sperm
These are lower fifth-percentile values from men whose partners conceived within 12 months. They are not absolute cut-offs separating fertile from infertile men.
**A. Semen volume**
This is the volume of the entire ejaculate.

blocks.title: Low volume may be associated with:

items.text: Incomplete sample collection.
Retrograde ejaculation.
Ejaculatory duct obstruction.
Congenital absence of the vas deferens in selected cases.
Androgen deficiency or other disorders affecting accessory gland function.

blocks.text: A low volume result should first be interpreted alongside the collection history and repeated when appropriate.
**B. Sperm concentration**
This is the number of sperm per millilitre of semen.
A concentration below 16 million/mL is below the WHO lower reference value.

items.text: Impaired spermatogenesis.
Varicocele in selected cases.
Hormonal disorders.
Undescended testes.
Genetic conditions.
Gonadotoxic medication or treatment.
Exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroid use.
Partial obstruction or other reproductive disorders.

blocks.text: **C. Total sperm number**
This is the total number of sperm in the entire ejaculate.
Calculate it as:
\[ \text{Total sperm number} = \text{Volume}\times\text{Concentration} \]
For example, a volume of 2 mL and a concentration of 10 million/mL gives:
\[ 2\times10=20\text{ million} \]
The total sperm number is therefore 20 million per ejaculate, below the WHO lower reference value of 39 million.
**D. Sperm motility**
Motility describes the proportion of sperm that move.

items.text: Progressive motility: Sperm move forward, either in a straight line or a large circle.
Non-progressive motility: Sperm move but do not progress effectively.
Immotile sperm: Sperm show no movement.

blocks.text: Total motility includes progressive and non-progressive motility.
Reduced motility may be associated with testicular dysfunction, infection or inflammation in selected cases, oxidative stress, recent illness or specimen-handling problems.
**E. Sperm morphology**
Morphology assesses sperm shape using strict laboratory criteria.

blocks.title: The laboratory assesses features such as:

items.text: Head shape and size.
Acrosomal region.
Midpiece.
Tail.
Cytoplasmic residues.

blocks.text: A normal morphology value of 4% means that 4% of assessed sperm meet the strict normal-form criteria. It does not mean that the remaining sperm are all incapable of fertilisation.
**F. Sperm vitality**
Vitality assesses whether sperm are alive, particularly when many are immotile.
This helps distinguish live but immotile sperm from dead sperm. A low vitality result may require further evaluation depending on the overall semen profile.
**G. Other laboratory findings**
The laboratory may also report pH, liquefaction, viscosity, appearance, round cells and other findings.

These results must be interpreted in context. For example, white blood cells may prompt evaluation for inflammation or infection when clinically indicated, but round cells alone do not establish an infection.

rows: No sperm detected in the ejaculate
Reduced proportion of sperm with normal morphology
Reduced concentration, motility and normal morphology
Extremely rare sperm detected only after examination of a concentrated specimen in the relevant laboratory context
Increased white blood cells in semen, conventionally more than 1 million peroxidase-positive leukocytes/mL

blocks.text: Important distinction: Azoospermia is not the same as oligozoospermia. In azoospermia, sperm are not detected in the ejaculate after appropriate laboratory assessment; in oligozoospermia, sperm are present but the concentration is reduced.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. How to interpret a semen analysis: worked cases

blocks.title: In an OSCE, use a systematic approach:

items.text: Check whether the sample was collected correctly.
Review volume and sperm concentration.
Calculate or review total sperm number.
Assess progressive and total motility.
Assess morphology and vitality.
Identify the abnormality and possible causes.
State the next investigation or management step.

blocks.text: LABORATORY REPORT
Interpretation: Reduced sperm concentration. The total sperm number is \(2.5\times8=20\) million per ejaculate, also below the WHO reference value.
Next steps: Repeat the analysis when indicated, review medications and illness history, and consider hormonal and male reproductive assessment.
LABORATORY REPORT
Interpretation: Both total and progressive motility are below the WHO lower reference values.
Next steps: Review sample handling, recent febrile illness and relevant medical history; repeat testing as appropriate and arrange further assessment.
LABORATORY REPORT
Interpretation: Azoospermia is suspected. Confirm according to laboratory protocol, including examination of a centrifuged sample where appropriate.
Next steps: Refer for male reproductive assessment, including examination, hormonal testing and selected genetic investigations. Differentiate obstructive from non-obstructive azoospermia.
LABORATORY REPORT
Interpretation: Semen volume is below the lower reference value. Concentration alone cannot determine the total sperm output.

Next steps: Confirm complete collection and repeat if indicated. If the abnormality persists, consider retrograde ejaculation, ejaculatory duct obstruction, androgen deficiency or other causes based on the clinical history.
LABORATORY REPORT
Interpretation: Normal morphology is below the WHO lower reference value, while the other listed parameters are within their reference limits.
Next steps: Interpret the result with the complete report and clinical context. Isolated abnormal morphology does not establish sterility or automatically require ICSI.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. Common causes of abnormal semen analysis

blocks.text: Think of causes in five broad categories.
1. Testicular causes
Undescended testes, testicular torsion, trauma, orchitis, genetic conditions, testicular cancer and damage from chemotherapy or radiotherapy.
2. Hormonal causes
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, pituitary disorders and suppression of LH and FSH by exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroids.
3. Obstructive causes
Congenital absence of the vas deferens, epididymal obstruction, ejaculatory duct obstruction or previous vasectomy.
4. Medical and lifestyle factors
Selected systemic illnesses, smoking, certain medications, reproductive toxin exposure and some cases of varicocele-associated sperm abnormalities.
5. Collection and laboratory factors
Incomplete collection, inappropriate abstinence interval, delayed processing, unsuitable temperature conditions or recent febrile illness.

subsections.subsection_title: 8. Further investigations after an abnormal result

blocks.text: The investigations depend on the severity and pattern of the abnormality.

rows: Abnormal initial result or suspected collection problem
Azoospermia, oligozoospermia, small testes or suspected hormonal dysfunction
Selected cases of suspected endocrine dysfunction
Persistent abnormalities, azoospermia or suspected structural disease
Palpable mass, uncertain examination or selected structural indications
Selected cases of severe sperm-production impairment
Congenital absence of the vas deferens or selected obstructive cases
Selected cases of suspected ejaculatory duct obstruction

blocks.text: Not every patient needs all these tests. Severe oligozoospermia and azoospermia warrant specialist evaluation, with genetic testing selected according to current guidance and the clinical findings.
Treatment depends on the cause, the severity of the abnormalities, the female partner's reproductive status and the couple's preferences.

items.text: Stop smoking and recreational drug use.
Avoid anabolic steroids and non-prescribed testosterone.
Review prescribed medication with the treating clinician.
Optimise weight, nutrition and chronic disease management.
Address relevant occupational exposures.
Manage erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction.
Provide counselling and realistic expectations.

blocks.text: Sperm development takes approximately 74 days, followed by epididymal maturation and transport. Consequently, changes in lifestyle or treatment may take several months to affect semen parameters.

rows: Specialist-directed gonadotrophin therapy or pulsatile GnRH in selected patients
Clinician-led review and specialist fertility management; recovery may take months or longer
Consider repair in selected infertile men with a palpable varicocele and abnormal semen parameters
Selected microsurgical reconstruction or sperm retrieval
Specialist assessment, cause-specific management and discussion of selected sperm-retrieval options
Treat the underlying cause and consider assisted reproductive techniques when needed
Consider IVF with ICSI where clinically appropriate

blocks.text: Important: Testosterone replacement should not be prescribed as fertility treatment in a man seeking conception because it can suppress sperm production.
Intrauterine insemination (IUI)
Prepared sperm is placed in the uterus around ovulation. It may be suitable for selected couples with mild male-factor infertility and favourable overall fertility findings.
In vitro fertilisation (IVF)
Eggs are collected and fertilised in the laboratory, with an embryo subsequently transferred into the uterus.
Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)
A single sperm is injected directly into an egg during IVF. It is commonly considered for significant male-factor infertility, selected sperm-retrieval cases or previous fertilisation failure.
ICSI does not guarantee fertilisation or pregnancy. Discuss the indication, costs, risks and potential genetic implications where relevant.
Q1. What are the WHO lower reference values for sperm concentration and total sperm number?
Model answer: Sperm concentration is 16 million/mL, and total sperm number is 39 million per ejaculate in the WHO sixth-edition reference data.
Q2. What is the difference between concentration and total sperm number?
Model answer: Concentration is the number of sperm per millilitre, while total sperm number is the concentration multiplied by the total semen volume.
Q3. Does one abnormal semen analysis establish infertility?
Model answer: No. Semen parameters vary between samples. The result should be interpreted in context, and repeat testing is often indicated when abnormalities are identified.
Q4. How do you confirm suspected azoospermia?
Model answer: Confirm the result using appropriate laboratory procedures, including examination of a centrifuged specimen when indicated, then investigate obstructive and non-obstructive causes.
Q5. Why might a man with normal sperm concentration still have infertility?
Model answer: Concentration is only one parameter. Motility, morphology, vitality, sexual function, sperm function and female reproductive factors may also influence conception.
Q6. What does a low semen volume suggest?

Model answer: Possible causes include incomplete collection, retrograde ejaculation, ejaculatory duct obstruction and androgen deficiency. The result should be confirmed and investigated according to the history.
Q7. What is the role of ICSI?
Model answer: ICSI involves injecting one sperm directly into an egg during IVF. It is useful in selected cases of significant male-factor infertility but does not guarantee a successful pregnancy.
Q8. Why should both partners be assessed?
Model answer: Male and female factors can coexist. Parallel evaluation helps identify the cause and select the most appropriate and timely treatment.

items.text: Failing to explain specimen collection properly.
Ignoring incomplete sample collection.
Confusing sperm concentration with total sperm number.
Treating WHO reference limits as absolute fertility cut-offs.
Assuming one abnormal result proves permanent infertility.
Forgetting to review testosterone and anabolic steroid use.
Ordering extensive genetic tests without appropriate indications.
Prescribing testosterone to a man actively seeking fertility.
Recommending ICSI automatically for every abnormal semen analysis.
Failing to investigate the female partner at the same time.
